newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexican official says peso as stable as mark, yen.
newsitem.headline: Mexican official says peso as stable as mark, yen.

text.p: Mexico's peso has become as stable as other currencies such as the German mark and the Japanese yen due to better fiscal and monetary discipline in Mexico, deputy finance minister Jose Sidaoui said on Thursday.
Speaking at the annual meeting of the Mexican Financial Executives Association (IMEF), Sidaoui added that interest rates had been able to fall for most of the year because of the greater stability.
After the financial crisis that began in December 1994, the Mexican currency was badly battered during 1995, but has shown greater stability this year, he said.

"The volatility that was seen in the exchange rate, the peso versus the dollar (in 1996), is similar to that which was seen in other international markets, for example, the mark against the dollar, and the yen against the dollar," Sidaoui said.
He said that the daily variation of the peso was rarely more than one percent at any time during the year.
During his speech, Sidaoui reiterated that the government would miss its target for inflation for 1996, which was originally set at 20.5 percent.
"Obviously that won't be reached. That was one of the objectives that won't be totally met," he said, but added that inflation was on a downward trend.
Inflation for 1996 is expected to come in at half of last year's rate of 52 percent.
- since the crisis, Mexican families have become, in the aggregate, net lenders rather than borrowers,
- the small current account deficit foreseen for 1997 could be financed by foreign direct investment,

- and the amount of the government's maturing external public debt, after reaching $41.4 billion in 1995 and falling to $16.0 billion in 1996, will drop to $9.0 billion in 1997, and an average of $10.0 billion in 1998 and 1999.
